_meta.description: Where this thesis breaks: the mechanisms that turn today's shortages into tomorrow's gluts, the historical cases, and a per-vertical read of how exposed each one is. Written 2026-09-05 at the owner's request.
_meta.why_this_exists: Every force in the Orientation is a demand story. A book built only on shortages has no way to see the reversal coming. Inflated prices pull forward investment; deglobalisation duplicates capacity in every bloc; high prices invite switching; and innovation thins the material out of the product. Each of these has ended a commodity cycle before.
_meta.scoring_note: glut_risk is a PROPOSED 1–5 score written by the analyst on 2026-09-05 from the evidence in each row. It is NOT the owner's judgment and is labelled as proposed wherever it renders. 5 = a glut is already visible or the capacity to create one is committed; 1 = no credible mechanism on a 5-year horizon.
_meta.verification: Historical figures attributed per row: lithium (INN, Forbes, Metal Tech News), polysilicon (Caixin, SMM, Yicai), LNG (OIES via Columbia CGEP; Ras Laffan strikes via Argus/Al Jazeera/CNBC), nickel (Antara, IDNFinancials), battery cells (CRU), steel (OECD Steel Outlook 2026, worldsteel), mining capex (McKinsey, Auspice), shipping (Clarksons via BIMCO). Not independently recomputed.

mechanisms.title: Over-investment from inflated prices
mechanisms.how: High prices are the signal that brings supply. In commodities the response arrives 3–7 years later, all at once, into a demand that has usually already adjusted. Inflationary episodes make this worse: capital is cheap in real terms and every project clears its hurdle.
mechanisms.tell: Capex / depreciation above 1.5× across a sector; announced capacity exceeding forecast demand; juniors funding at the top; 'this time is different' language about structural deficits — which is also the language of this dashboard.
mechanisms.lag: 3–7 years for mines and yards; 2–3 for processing plants; 12–18 months for shale.

mechanisms.title: Deglobalisation duplicates capacity
mechanisms.how: If every bloc insists on its own separation plant, enrichment cascade, transformer factory and shipyard, the world ends up with more capacity than one integrated market needed. Strategic premiums pay for it on the way up; overcapacity is the bill on the way down. This is the mechanism specific to THIS cycle and the one least visible in historical analogs.
mechanisms.tell: The same product being built in the US, EU, Japan and Australia simultaneously against one demand pool; policy floors (CFDs, offtakes, tariffs) that keep uneconomic capacity running.
mechanisms.lag: The policy-funded plants take 2027–2030 to arrive together.

mechanisms.title: China exports its overcapacity
mechanisms.how: Chinese overcapacity does not stay in China. Steel, solar, batteries and now chemicals are exported below Western cost, which caps the price the reshored capacity can earn. Tariffs redirect the flow; they do not remove it.
mechanisms.tell: Record Chinese export volumes into third markets; Western producers' pricing power failing despite tariffs; trade-remedy filings.
mechanisms.lag: Already operating in steel, solar and batteries.

mechanisms.title: Switching — the buyer changes material
mechanisms.how: A high enough price for long enough teaches the customer to use something else. Aluminium for copper in cable and busbar; sodium for lithium in stationary storage; magnet-free motors; LFP for NMC. The switch is slow, then permanent.
mechanisms.tell: Substitute reaching cost parity; OEM design wins announced for the substitute; the incumbent's demand forecast quietly cut.
mechanisms.lag: Design cycles: 2–4 years in autos, faster in storage.

mechanisms.title: Innovation thins the material out
mechanisms.how: Thrifting, recycling and process change reduce intensity per unit. PGM loadings per catalyst fell for two decades; silver per solar cell keeps falling; HTS cable moves more power per kilogram of copper.
mechanisms.tell: Intensity-of-use falling faster than the volume forecast assumes.
mechanisms.lag: Continuous; shows up as forecasts missing on the demand side.

mechanisms.title: Policy reversal
mechanisms.how: The floors and credits that underwrite reshoring were written by legislatures that can rewrite them. 45X has already been amended once (OBBBA added a critical-minerals taper). A floor that is out of the money — the MP CFD since 2026-02 — costs the state nothing until it is needed, and that is when it will be questioned.
mechanisms.tell: Budget reconciliation language; floors going into the money; program renewals lapsing.

analogs.what_happened: Capex peaked in 2012–14 across mining and oil & gas and did not return for a decade. Five mining cycles since 2000 with peaks in 2001, 2007, 2010, 2013 and early 2015, each followed by an abrupt drop.
analogs.lesson: The under-investment this dashboard leans on is the AFTERMATH of the last glut. The mechanism that created the gap can recreate the glut.

analogs.what_happened: Carbonate peaked ~$80,000/t in 2022-11 and fell ~89% to $8,000–9,000/t by 2025-08. Surplus ~175kt LCE in 2023, ~154kt in 2024. Core Lithium suspended Finniss; Pilbara cut guidance; Albemarle and SQM trimmed. By 2026 analysts are calling a deficit again.
analogs.lesson: A 3–5-year mine lead time turned 2021 price signals into 2024 supply. The cure for the glut was the glut. Sodium-ion reaching LFP cost parity in late 2026 is the switching risk on the recovery.
analogs.source: INN; Forbes; Metal Tech News; Canaccord via IndexBox

analogs.what_happened: China's solar manufacturing capacity reached ~1,200 GW in 2025 against global demand near half that; polysilicon utilisation 44% in 2025; prices below cash cost; Tongwei's first annual loss since listing (¥7.0bn), four leaders ~¥19bn combined losses in 2024; inventories ~570–600kt entering 2026.
analogs.lesson: Policy-directed capacity does not stop at the market-clearing quantity. The Western 'reshored' solar chain competes against this.

analogs.what_happened: Global excess capacity above 680Mt in 2025 (OECD); Chinese exports a record 131Mt in 2025, nearly double in three years, increasingly as semi-finished product to route around finished-goods tariffs.
analogs.lesson: The dumping mechanism in its mature form. Section 232 protects US mills' price, not their volume growth.

analogs.what_happened: ~4,800 GWh of planned Chinese cell capacity against ~1,000 GWh of demand; utilisation 50–55% across the sector even as top-tier plants ran full; surplus cells exported to Europe and North America; Beijing moved to curb price wars and overseas expansion in 2026.
analogs.lesson: Downstream overcapacity pulls the glut upstream into lithium, nickel, graphite and copper foil.

analogs.period: 2022–25 boom in Indonesian supply, 2025–26 quota cuts
analogs.what_happened: Indonesian ore quotas cut from 272Mt (2024) toward 150Mt (2025) and a 2026 target of 250–260Mt, ~34% below the 2025 target, to hold prices near the $18–19k/t break-even of Indonesian projects after a year in the $14–16k range.
analogs.lesson: A single state can create AND unwind a glut by decree. Class 1 nickel outside Indonesia (SMM, Western refiners) is priced off Jakarta's quota decisions.

analogs.what_happened: The base case into 2026 was a multi-year glut: Qatar North Field East (32 Mtpa) plus US Gulf Coast projects; OIES put 2030 capacity 6–13% above demand. Then Iranian strikes on Ras Laffan on 2026-03-18/19 damaged two trains and a GTL plant, removed ~17% of Qatar's capacity (~12.8 Mtpa), triggered force majeure still being extended in July, and pushed North Field expansion to 2027. A six-month delay plus damage could cut 2028 additions by ~28 Mtpa.
analogs.lesson: The glut was DEFERRED, not cancelled. Capacity under construction still arrives; the timing shifted right by a year or two. Read LNG-carrier order books (40% of fleet) against this.
analogs.source: Columbia CGEP; OIES; Argus; Al Jazeera; CNBC; EnergyNow

analogs.what_happened: Orderbook 17% of fleet at Q1 2026, highest since 2011. Yards are booked to 2028–30 and Korean groups are adding US docks. The last time the ratio was this high the following eight years were a yard depression.
analogs.lesson: Yards are the purest capacity industry in this book. The offset today is fleet age and the shadow fleet, which the last cycle did not have.

verticals.evidence: Just lived one: −89% peak to trough, ~175kt LCE surplus in 2023, curtailments across the cost curve. Chinese cell overcapacity sits downstream. Sodium-ion at GWh scale (CATL, BYD) with LFP cost parity projected late 2026 — 20–30% of stationary storage by 2030 in vendor projections.
verticals.counter: Supply curtailments and project deferrals flipped consensus to a 2026 deficit; the recovery could be sharp precisely because the glut was so deep.
verticals.watch: Sodium-ion share of new storage tenders; Chinese lepidolite restarts above $12k/t; Pilbara/MinRes restart decisions.

verticals.evidence: Third LNG wave committed; OIES 2030 capacity 6–13% above demand. Qatar strikes removed ~12.8 Mtpa and pushed NFE to 2027 — a deferral. LNG carriers 40% of fleet on order are the shipping expression of the same bet.
verticals.counter: Ras Laffan damage and force majeure; Asian coal-to-gas switching at low prices absorbs volume (the 2026 price cap spurred demand).
verticals.watch: NFE first cargo date; US FID pace; JKM-TTF spread; carrier order cancellations.

verticals.evidence: 680Mt+ global steel overcapacity; China exported 131Mt in 2025. Polysilicon and battery-cell chains at ~45–55% utilisation. The reshored Western plant competes against this on price even behind tariffs.
verticals.counter: Industrial gases are on-site, sole-source and contracted — largely immune. Section 232 holds US steel PRICE.
verticals.watch: Chinese semi-finished steel exports; EU CBAM; US mill utilisation.

verticals.evidence: New potash capacity arriving (BHP Jansen first production guided 2026–27 — NOT re-verified this pass) into a market where Belarusian and Russian volumes have re-routed rather than disappeared; nitrogen capacity additions in the US and Middle East.
verticals.counter: Phosphate remains structurally tight (Morocco concentration, China export curbs).
verticals.watch: Jansen ramp; Belaruskali export routes; urea capacity additions.

verticals.evidence: The transformer shortage is being answered: ~$2bn of North American capacity (Hitachi Energy, Siemens Energy and others) online by 2028; Wood Mackenzie projects the US LPT supply gap closing from ~30% to ~5% by 2030. Shortage pricing normalises when it lands.
verticals.counter: Grid capex is a 10–15-year programme; demand outruns capacity additions in most forecasts through 2030.
verticals.watch: Transformer lead times (2–4 yrs today); order intake at Hitachi Energy/Siemens Energy; utility capex guidance.

verticals.evidence: OPEC+ spare capacity; US shale's short lag; EV penetration and efficiency thin demand growth. VLCC order book ~30% is the tanker-side version.
verticals.counter: Tanker fleet age 14.3 yrs and 23% shadow share mean effective fleet growth under 3%; refining closures tighten product.
verticals.watch: OPEC+ quota path; US rig response; shadow-fleet enforcement.

verticals.n: Tech metals (Ga, Ge, Sb, W, Ti)
verticals.evidence: Tiny markets. Policy-funded Western capacity (DPA awards, EXIM, Project Vault) can overshoot demand measured in thousands of tonnes; and China can re-flood on the 2026-11-27 suspension expiry or by simply lifting licensing.
verticals.counter: Stockpiling (Project Vault, up to $12bn) is designed to absorb exactly this.
verticals.watch: 2026-11-27; antimony Rotterdam price vs Chinese domestic; Stibnite FID (H2 2026).

verticals.evidence: Parallel separation capacity being built in the US, Australia, EU and Japan against one Western magnet demand pool; magnet-free and reduced-Dy motor designs; China's 91% refining share can undercut any of it. The MP floor at $110/kg socialises the downside — until the floor is in the money and questioned.
verticals.counter: Western HREE separation is still ~zero; Seadrift did not happen. The glut risk is 2029+, not now.
verticals.watch: NdPr vs $110 floor; 2026-11-10 (0.1% rule); Western separation plants actually commissioned.

verticals.evidence: Demand-side glut: BEVs need no autocatalyst; thrifting reduces loadings; recycling supplies ~20–25% of Pt/Pd. South African supply is constrained, so this is a slow demand fade rather than a supply flood.
verticals.counter: Hydrogen (PEM electrolysers, fuel cells) is the platinum demand offset — long-dated and policy-dependent.
verticals.watch: ICE share of new sales; recycling volumes; SA production.

verticals.evidence: The glut that exists is in SMELTING, not mining: China ~50% of smelter output, TC/RCs near zero in 2024 — a processing glut that this book previously read only as a mine-supply signal. Aluminium substitution in cable and busbar at high price ratios; HTS moves more power per kg.
verticals.counter: Mine supply lead times of 15–20 years in democracies; no committed wave of new mines.
verticals.watch: TC/RC benchmarks; Cu/Al price ratio; aluminium share of new HV cable awards.

verticals.evidence: Enrichment is being rebuilt in the US (Centrus, $900M), Europe (Urenco, Orano) and elsewhere at once against SMR demand that has slipped before. Kazatomprom flexes output by decree.
verticals.counter: Restart and life-extension demand is firm; the 2028 waiver cliff is a hard deadline for Western SWU.
verticals.watch: SMR FIDs actually taken; Centrus Piketon first capacity (2029); Kazatomprom guidance.

verticals.evidence: No credible over-build mechanism: capacity is local, fragmented and regulated.

indicators: Sector capex / depreciation (above ~1.5× = building the next glut)
Announced capacity vs forecast demand, by bloc — count the duplicates
Utilisation rates (China polysilicon 44%, cells 50–55% = glut already here)
Price vs marginal cost — a price far above the 90th-percentile cost is an invitation
Substitute cost parity dates (sodium-ion late 2026; Al/Cu ratio)
Chinese export volumes into third markets (steel 131Mt 2025)
Order book % of fleet, net of age and shadow absorption (ships)
Policy floors going into the money — the moment they cost the state something
